chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Financial Markets Matter to Your Job

lessons.title: What Financial Markets Are and Why Every Employee Should Understand Them

body.text: Financial markets are not a separate world that only the finance team visits. They set your company's borrowing cost, your raw material bill, the value of your ESOPs and the growth of your EPF balance. You are already inside them, whether you trade or not.

children.text: Most employees meet financial markets in fragments: a Sensex headline on the morning news, a CFO slide about "rate headwinds", a vendor invoice that jumped because the rupee weakened. This lesson gives you one frame that ties those fragments together, so the next time markets come up in a meeting, you know what is being discussed and why it lands on your desk.
What a Financial Market Actually Is

markDefs.definition: Any organised venue, physical or electronic, where buyers and sellers trade financial claims such as shares, bonds, currencies and commodity contracts.
The process through which a market arrives at a price for an asset, based on the combined buying and selling decisions of all participants.

children.text: A
financial market

is any organised venue where buyers and sellers trade financial claims: shares, bonds, currencies and commodity contracts. Markets do two jobs that matter to every business. First, they move money from people who have it to people who need it. Second, they perform
price discovery
, which means they continuously set a price for money, risk and ownership that the rest of the economy uses as a reference.

That second job is the one non finance employees underestimate. When your bank quotes a loan rate, when procurement negotiates a steel contract, when a founder hears that listed peers trade at 40 times earnings, every one of them is borrowing a price that was discovered in a market.

children.text: The Four Markets You Will Keep Hearing About

body.caption: The Four Core Financial Markets in India
headers: Where It Shows Up at Work

cells: Equity
Shares of companies
NSE, BSE
ESOP values, fundraising, company valuation, peer benchmarking
Debt
Government securities, corporate bonds, commercial paper
RBI's NDS-OM platform, NSE and BSE debt segments, over the counter between banks and institutions
Loan interest rates, working capital cost, returns on surplus cash
Currency
Rupee against the dollar, euro and other currencies

Import bills, export receipts, overseas vendor payments, foreign travel budgets
Commodity
Gold, crude oil, base metals, agri produce
MCX, NCDEX, NSE commodity segment

body.text: You do not need to trade in any of these markets for them to affect you. A family-owned company that has never issued a share or a bond still pays a loan rate set off the debt market, buys inputs priced off commodity markets and pays foreign vendors at a rate set in the currency market.

body.title: Name the Market
body.question: Your procurement head reports that aluminium prices have risen 9% this month, and the finished goods team wants to revise its price list. Which market is driving this conversation?
body.explanation: Aluminium is a base metal, and its price is discovered in commodity markets, including MCX in India and global exchanges such as the LME. The price you negotiate with a supplier is anchored to that market price.

children.text: Primary vs Secondary Markets: The Distinction That Clears Most Confusion

Every market has two layers. In the primary market, a company or government issues a new security and receives the money. In the secondary market, investors trade that existing security among themselves, and the issuer receives nothing.

columns.label: Primary Market
points: New securities are created and sold for the first time
Money goes to the issuing company or government
Examples: an IPO, a QIP, a company issuing new bonds, RBI auctioning government securities
Happens occasionally, as a specific event

columns.label: Secondary Market
points: Existing securities change hands between investors
The company receives no money from these trades
Examples: buying Infosys shares on NSE through Zerodha, a mutual fund selling a bond to a bank

body.label: The One-Question Test
body.context: If yes, it was a primary market transaction. If no, it was a secondary market trade between investors.

children.text: This is why a sharp fall in your employer's share price does not empty the company bank account. The sellers and buyers are investors trading with each other. The effect on the company is real, but indirect.

body.title: So How Does a Falling Share Price Actually Hurt a Company?

children.text: The company's cash does not move when its shares trade lower, but four things change:
Future fundraising gets more expensive.
If the company later raises equity through a QIP or rights issue, it must issue more shares to raise the same amount, diluting existing shareholders more.
ESOPs lose their pull.
Stock options are worth less when the share price falls, which weakens retention exactly when morale is already under pressure.
Acquisitions paid in shares cost more.
A company using its own shares as currency to buy another business has to hand over more of them.
Pledged promoter shares come under pressure.
If promoters have borrowed against their shares, lenders may demand more collateral or sell the pledged shares, which can push the price lower still.

body.title: Where Does the Money Go?
body.question: Your company's shares change hands 2 lakh times on NSE today. How much money does the company receive from those trades?
options: The full value of all trades
A small commission on each trade
Nothing, because these are secondary market trades between investors
Only the value of shares bought by foreign investors
body.explanation: Every one of those trades is between an investor selling existing shares and an investor buying them. The company raised its money when it first issued those shares in the primary market. Brokerage and exchange charges go to the broker and the exchange, not to the company.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: When RBI auctions new government securities to banks, that transaction takes place in the ___ market.
body.explanation: The government is issuing brand new securities and receiving the money, which makes it a primary market transaction. When those banks later sell the securities to each other or to mutual funds, that is the secondary market.

children.text: Worked Example: One Import Bill, Two Exchange Rates

A Pune-based auto components maker imports machine parts worth USD 100,000 every quarter. The purchase was budgeted when the rupee was at ₹83 per dollar. By the time payment is due, the rupee has weakened to ₹87.

body.caption: The rupee cost of any dollar invoice depends on the exchange rate on the day you pay, not the day you ordered.

stats.label: Overrun per Year
stats.context: If the rate stays at ₹87 for four quarters

children.text: Nobody in procurement negotiated badly. The currency market moved. That ₹16 lakh still shows up in the P&L as margin pressure, and someone in a review meeting will ask why. Chapter 4 covers how businesses hedge exactly this risk.

body.title: Your Turn: One RBI Decision, One Loan
body.prompt: Your company has a ₹20 crore working capital loan linked to an external benchmark, the RBI repo rate. After a rate hike, the loan's interest rate rises by 0.50 percentage points. What is the extra annual interest cost, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: ₹20 crore × 0.50% = ₹0.10 crore = ₹10 lakh a year. A single RBI decision added ₹10 lakh to your company's annual interest bill before anyone inside the company made a single decision. Chapter 3 explains how this transmission works.

body.title: The Morning After Results
body.scenario: You are an HR business partner at a listed Bengaluru IT services company. The stock fell 11% on NSE the morning after quarterly results because the company cut its revenue guidance. By lunch, three managers have messaged you. One team is asking whether the company is in trouble. Two employees want to know whether they should sell the shares they received from vested ESOPs.
body.prompt: What do you say to them, and what do you avoid saying?
body.modelAnswer: Start by separating the share price from the company's finances. The fall happened in the secondary market, between investors reacting to lower guidance. The company's cash position did not change overnight, so a price fall on its own is not evidence that the company is in trouble. Point people to what the company has actually disclosed: the results and investor presentation filed on NSE and BSE. On the ESOP question, do not tell anyone to buy, hold or sell. That is a personal investment decision, and HR is not a SEBI-registered adviser. Do remind them that, as employees of a listed company, they may be covered by the company's insider trading code, and the trading window may still be closed, since under SEBI's insider trading rules it typically reopens only 48 hours after results are made public. They should check with the compliance team before transacting. Finally, flag to leadership that employees are anxious, because a clear internal message from the business does more than individual reassurance.

body.label: NSE India: Live Market and Company Announcements
body.description: Look up your own employer, a major customer or a key supplier. Check the share price trend and the corporate announcements section to see what the company has disclosed recently.

cards.definition: An organised venue, physical or electronic, where buyers and sellers trade financial claims such as shares, bonds, currencies and commodity contracts.
The process through which a market sets a price for an asset, based on the combined decisions of all buyers and sellers.
Where new securities are issued for the first time and the issuer receives the money, for example an IPO or a new bond issue.
Where existing securities trade between investors. The issuing company receives nothing from these trades.
How easily an asset can be bought or sold quickly without moving its price much. Nifty 50 shares are highly liquid; a small unlisted bond is not.
Where raw materials such as gold, crude oil, metals and agri produce are traded. In India, mainly MCX and NCDEX.

points: Financial markets move money from those who have it to those who need it, and set reference prices for money, risk and ownership
The four markets that matter at work are equity, debt, currency and commodity, and each one reaches a different desk in your company
In the primary market the issuer receives money; in the secondary market investors trade with each other and the company receives nothing
A falling share price does not drain company cash, but it makes fundraising costlier, weakens ESOPs and can pressure pledged promoter shares
Small market moves translate into real rupees: a ₹4 move in the dollar rate or a 0.50 percentage point rate hike can add lakhs to annual costs
